## The question

Functional linear regression is a natural tool when predictors are curves
rather than finite-dimensional vectors.

> **When can multiple functional regression tasks borrow strength from one
> another without forcing their underlying representations to be identical?**

## Why exact sharing can be too restrictive

For task \(m\), we consider

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{*(m)}(t)
=
\boldsymbol A^{*(m)}
\boldsymbol\alpha^{*(m)}(t).
$$

Classical shared-representation models impose

$$
\boldsymbol A^{*(1)}
=
\cdots
=
\boldsymbol A^{*(M)}.
$$

We instead allow the representations to be similar but heterogeneous.

## Functional regression changes the geometry

For a perturbation \(\boldsymbol f\), define the prediction seminorm

$$
\|\boldsymbol f\|_{X^{(m)}}^2
=
\left\langle
\boldsymbol f,
\mathcal C^{(m)}
\boldsymbol f
\right\rangle.
$$

If

$$
\mathcal C\phi_k=\mu_k\phi_k,
\qquad
f=\sum_{k\ge1}c_k\phi_k,
$$

then

$$
\|f\|_X^2
=
\sum_{k\ge1}\mu_kc_k^2,
$$

whereas

$$
\|f\|_{L_2}^2
=
\sum_{k\ge1}c_k^2.
$$

Thus, two perturbations that are equally large in \(L_2\) geometry may
have very different predictive consequences.

## Statistical formulation

For \(m\in[M]\),

$$
Y_i^{(m)}
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\int_{\mathcal T}
X_{ij}^{(m)}(t)
\beta_j^{*(m)}(t)\,dt
+
\varepsilon_i^{(m)}.
$$

We assume

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{*(m)}(t)
=
\boldsymbol A^{*(m)}
\boldsymbol\alpha^{*(m)}(t),
\qquad
\boldsymbol A^{*(m)}\in\mathbb O_{p,r}.
$$

## Similar rather than identical representations

There exists a central representation
\(\overline{\boldsymbol A}\) such that

$$
\left\|
P_{\boldsymbol A^{*(m)}}
-
P_{\overline{\boldsymbol A}}
\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le h
$$

for informative tasks \(m\in\mathcal S\).

The case \(h=0\) corresponds to exact representation sharing.

## Two ways to learn across tasks

### Penalized empirical risk minimization

The first approach combines

$$
\text{prediction loss}
+
\text{functional roughness}
+
\text{representation similarity}.
$$

A task-specific refitting step subsequently adapts the joint estimator to
each individual task.

### Spectral aggregation

The second approach follows

$$
\text{single-task pilots}
\rightarrow
\text{robust aggregation}
\rightarrow
\text{SVD}
\rightarrow
\text{central representation}
\rightarrow
\text{task-specific refitting}.
$$

## What does the theory tell us?

Suppressing constants and logarithmic factors, the estimation error has
the schematic form

$$
\text{error}
\lesssim
\underbrace{
\sigma\sqrt{\frac{rp}{n|\mathcal S|}}
}_{\text{cross-task gain}}
+
\underbrace{
\sigma\sqrt{\frac{r\,d_K(\eta)}{n}}
}_{\text{functional estimation}}
+
\underbrace{
K^{-\tau}
+
\eta^{1/2}K^{(d-\nu)_+}
}_{\text{approximation and smoothing}}
+
\underbrace{
\sqrt r\,h
}_{\text{heterogeneity}}
+
\underbrace{
\text{contamination}
}_{\epsilon}.
$$

The exact theorem contains task-specific signal-strength terms and
additional logarithmic factors; the display above is intended only to
highlight the statistical structure.

A key safeguard is that the final estimator is controlled by

$$
\text{multi-task error}
\wedge
\text{single-task error}.
$$

::: {.callout-note}
## A central design principle

Borrow information when tasks are compatible, but retain a single-task
fallback when they are not.
:::

## Why prediction geometry matters in refitting

Coefficient-space distance such as

$$
\|B-B_0\|_F
$$

does not directly reflect how a perturbation affects prediction.

The relevant functional geometry combines prediction and smoothness:

$$
\|\beta_B-\beta_{B_0}\|_X^2
+
\eta\|\beta_B\|_R^2.
$$

## What I learned from this project

This project changed how I think about multi-task learning in functional
models in several ways.

First, transferring finite-dimensional multi-task ideas to functional data
is not merely a matter of replacing vectors by basis coefficients. The
covariance operator changes the relevant statistical geometry.

Second, representation similarity alone is not sufficient for successful
multi-task learning. The tasks must also be sufficiently diverse to reveal
the latent representation.

Third, robustness and adaptivity are closely related design goals. A useful
multi-task procedure should exploit cross-task structure when it is present,
while retaining a reasonable fallback when the structure weakens.

Finally, the analysis requires functional approximation, empirical
prediction geometry, representation perturbation, and cross-task
concentration to work together.
